paper_title: ReproBridge: Building Reproducibility into ML Research Artifacts

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Reproducing machine learning experiments requires reconstructing procedures from information scattered across papers, released code, and supporting artifacts. For coding agents, reproduction success can therefore depend on their ability to fill in missing details, rather than on the released artifacts alone. We ask whether preserving recovered procedures and decisions improves subsequent independent reproduction. We define a standardized artifact design comprising a refined codebase, environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide, and introduce ReproBridge, an agent workflow for constructing these refined reproducible artifacts. ReproBridge-Bench provides 1,029 tasks from 387 experiments across 36 papers, anchored by five human-verified reference scores per task. Agents attempt tasks in fresh sessions with raw code or refined artifacts; a separate Auditor checks execution evidence. Across four evaluated models, refined artifacts raise mean reproduction success from 76.4% to 92.6% and reduce downstream API spending by 19.7% on average. The cross-model success-rate spread narrows from 21.6 to 3.9 percentage points, with all four models achieving mean success rates above 90%. Removing any component reduces success in the ablation study, with the largest losses from code and environment removal. These results suggest that preserving execution knowledge helps even models with lower raw-code success reproduce experiments more reliably and at lower API cost.

Introduction Reproducing machine learning experiment often requires recovering details that its paper and released code leave implicit. reproducer may resolve incompatible dependencies, identify the intended configuration, repair data loader, and work out how run outputs become reported score. Even successful attempt can leave these decisions buried in conversations or shell histories, forcing the next reproducer to repeat the investigation. Code release is an essential starting point (Pineau et al., 2021); preserving the procedure recovered during execution is further step toward reusable research artifacts (Stodden et al., 2016). Coding-agent benchmarks expose this reconstruction burden through unresolved dependencies and misidentified outputs (Siegel et al., 2024), missing implementation details (Xiang et al., 2025), and plans that never become completed experiments (Starace et al., 2025). Consulting cited papers can recover some missing details (Zhao et al., 2026b), but successful execution may still depend on knowledge capable agent supplies implicitly. How much does reproduction success depend on released artifacts, and how much on the reproducers ability to compensate for missing details? Here, reproduction means independently re-executing machine-learning experiments using authorreleased materials, targeting numerically compatible measurements. Research artifacts comprise the code, data, checkpoints, environment specifications, and documentation supporting study. Our hypothesis is that preserving the procedures and decisions recovered during reproduction can improve computational reproducibility. Dependency resolution can become an installation procedure; experiment discovery, dedicated launcher; and correction, documented choice with its justification and affected tasks. We study this hypothesis through three contributions. 1Project page: https://wyyyb.github.io/reprobridge_website/ ReproBridge: Building Reproducibility into ML Research Artifacts Figure 1 Preserving reproduction work for reuse. (a) ReproBridge turns paper and raw codebase into refined reproducible artifact (RRA) with code, environment setup, launchers, and guide. (b,c) Hollow blue (Raw) and filled green (Refined) circles show mean success and Reproducer API spending over three evaluations; dashed lines connect the two conditions for each model. Gain is the success difference (percentage points); cost reduction is relative to Raw. These procedures improve success and reduce reconstruction effort. Artifact design. We standardize refined reproducible artifact with four components: refined codebase, environment setup, experiment launchers, and reproduction guide (Figure 1; Section 3.2). Together they preserve executable procedures and the reasons for their settings and repairs. Component removals test the contribution of each part, while an ordinary-outputs control tests reuse of code, scripts, and logs without the standardized handoff. Construction workflow. ReproBridge constructs these artifacts from paper and its official repository (Section 3.1). Humans define the workflow, delivery standards, and protocols; agents specify experiments, prepare and execute them, and preserve the resulting procedures through review and packaging. Subsequent reuse is evaluated in fresh Reproducer sessions that receive either the raw codebase or the refined artifact. Benchmark and empirical evaluation. ReproBridge-Bench provides 1,029 tasks from 387 experiments across 36 papers, with five human-verified reference scores per task (Section 2). Numerical compatibility is assessed against observed executions and their variability; separate Auditor checks execution evidence because matching numbers alone can conceal substituted measurements. Across four coding agents, refined artifacts improve success by 5.5 to 23.2 pp and reduce downstream API spending by 16.8% to 23.7%. Robustness analyses, component ablations, case studies, and human validation of the integrity checks examine the scope and mechanisms of these gains (Section 4). 2. Problem formulation and ReproBridge-Bench 2.1. Execution deviations and reference variation task specifies the data, model configuration, training or evaluation procedure, and reporting statistic to reproduce. The papers stated setup takes precedence over conflicting code. Let 𝜇 be the expected value of that statistic when the specified experiment is faithfully executed. The published score is one observation, not an error-free value of 𝜇. ReproBridge: Building Reproducibility into ML Research Artifacts For an attempt producing measurement 𝑌 , we write 𝑌 = 𝜇 + 𝐷 + 𝜀. Here 𝐷 is the shift in expectation from execution choices departing from the specified experiment, and 𝜀 is zero-mean variation conditional on them. This working model draws on the distinction between systematic and random effects in measurement (Joint Committee for Guides in Metrology, 2020; Taylor and Kuyatt, 1994). Stochastic training can vary between runs (Nagarajan et al., 2018). Independent repetitions can reduce uncertainty about the mean of fixed procedure (Bouthillier et al., 2021), but do not remove persistent shift 𝐷. ReproBridge aims to reduce 𝐷 by preserving procedures and decisions for faithful execution, while 𝜀 remains. We use five human-verified reference observations of the same statistic per task. Assuming faithful and independent reference executions (𝐷 = 0), their mean estimates 𝜇, and their spread characterizes 𝜀. prediction interval accommodates uncertainty in that estimated center and variation in new observation 𝑌 (National Institute of Standards and Technology, n.d.). Section 2.3 describes collection and verification. Numerical compatibility is combined with the execution-integrity checks in Section 4.1: nearby number alone does not show that the intended experiment was performed. 2.2. Selection and units of analysis The collection targets main experimental results with accessible official implementations. The sampling manifest starts with 742 ICML 2026 Spotlight papers, identifies 241 with code and nonpurely-theoretical content, and randomly samples 50. Excluding six for artifact or code availability, four for compute requirements, and four for closed-model access yields 36 retained test papers. Figure 2 summarizes their research areas and paired reproduction gains. ReproBridge and evaluation workflows were developed on ten papers, five from NeurIPS 2026 and five from ICLR 2026, scored under the same task, reference, and audit conventions and reported separately in Appendix D.7. task is one own-method measurement in main table, identified by dataset, metric, reporting statistic, and location; selected main-table variants are retained. Baselines, stand-alone ablations, figures, and appendix-only results are excluded. An experiment can emit several task scores. The 36 papers yield 1,463 curated tasks from 502 experiments. The remaining 434 tasks distinguish numerical disagreement from execution and resource barriers. 2.3. Reference collection and task verification The reference protocol specifies five human reproducers on separate servers, starting from the same pinned raw commit with separate execution directories and coding-agent sessions. They must not reuse another participants generated scripts or measurements, refined artifacts, or downstream reproduction traces. Coding-agent assistance is permitted, but humans inspect the scripts, configurations, edits, and measurement extraction actually used. Before aggregation, the five reproducers execution setups were cross-verified against the papers specified setup and the common task definition. Each reference observation measures the specified task statistic: multiseed mean or best-of-𝑁 statistic is one observation, not interchangeable with single-seed scores. Verifiers must fix unspecified repetition and seed choices before inspecting scores, and must not tune procedures or repeat valid measurements until they approach the published value. Diagnostic runs and corrected reruns are recorded separately with reasons for replacement; numerical disagreement alone does not justify discarding valid execution. Scope and information access The evaluated set contains 631 full-procedure and 398 evaluation-only tasks (730 GPU, 299 CPU-only). Evaluating an explicitly permitted official checkpoint does not require repeating its training. Evaluation alone cannot establish completion of training task. All eight downstream conditions use the same task categories and numerical thresholds, applied outside the Reproducer session. Published targets remain visible in the paper and task specification; the Auditor checks that submitted values come from new executions. Session instructions withhold the reference information, alternative repository condition, and other agents run directories. ReproBridge: artifact design and construction ReproBridge turns reproduction work into an artifact that later researcher or agent can use without access to the construction conversation. The handoff comprises refined code, environment setup, experiment launchers, and reproduction guide. Its construction workflow preserves the evidence behind execution choices as well as the executable steps themselves. 3.1. Recoveries include 348 numerical mismatches, 210 unexecuted tasks due to execution or resource barriers (Not run), and 255 audit-invalid numerical matches. These records suggest two complementary contributions: completing ambiguous or incomplete measurement specifications and preserving executable procedures for reuse. Completing and clarifying measurement specifications. In Mixture of Concept Bottleneck Experts (De Santis et al., 2026), the reduction of multiple tree-edit distances is unspecified, and the released code lacks collector for Table 1. Sonnet 5s raw attempt sums the four distances, reporting 60 rather than 15. The refined artifact resolves this ambiguity by specifying the per-expression mean and supplying the collector; the later attempt reports 15. SCIQLs released code similarly leaves the mapping from run outputs to table entries incomplete; the refined artifact specifies the output field and aggregation across criteria and seeds. Such clarification and experiment-to-result mapping together represent about 35% of the case-review attribution distribution. Recovered configurations become executable: HELIX. For HELIX (Zhang et al., 2026a), Opus 5 restores the papers architecture on raw code but retains the shipped batch size and learning rate. The refined artifact identifies repository revision matching that architecture, records it as the source of the adopted settings, and exposes them through launcher. later attempt produces numerically compatible MAEs for both illustrated tasks. The guide records the evidence for the choice, and the launcher makes it reusable (Appendix D.5). compatible environment transfers across sessions: WBMM. For six COCO tasks in WBMM (Song et al., 2026), Sonnet 4.6s raw attempt fails to install compatible vision-library stack for H100. The refined artifact preserves the dependency versions, build prerequisite, and source-build route for the target architecture. The later session executes all six tasks without code patch; its box and mask AP values agree numerically with the reported targets. This case shows how an environment repair can become reusable installation procedure (Appendix D.5). Fixing bugs in the released code. In Effective Model Pruning (Wang et al., 2026), the released loader silently labels all 10,000 TinyImageNet validation images as one class. During construction, ReproBridge adds script organizing images by their true labels and launcher check requiring prepared data. In paired Gemini 3.8 Flash runs, ResNet-18 validation loss changes from 8.898 on raw code to 2.288 with the refined artifact, close to the papers 2.303. Modelpaper sessions changing code downstream fall from 113/144 to 54/144, and median time to first scored execution decreases for every model (Figure 6, right). Together with lower token use, this indicates less reconstruction. Explicit procedures also help the model that built them. Clearer code organization and explicit execution decisions can reduce repeated search and context demands, even for the model that built the artifact. In ETTFS (Che et al., 2026), the raw Opus 5 attempt searches 6,377 lines of Python for measurement code absent from the release. The refined artifact organizes the added measurement code into dedicated profiling module, launcher that sequences training and profiling, and documented output fields. fresh Opus 5 session follows this structure and completes previously blocked measurement. Remaining failures. Failures shared by both handoffs mainly reflect papercode setup mismatches, typographical errors in the paper, or experimental variability placing measurements outside the compatibility interval. Refinement can also preserve or introduce incorrect experimental choices. 11 ReproBridge: Building Reproducibility into ML Research Artifacts The 136 reversals from raw success to refined failure comprise 84 numerical mismatches, 31 resource/access failures, 11 audit-invalid matches, and 10 execution blockers. AuxiliaryMCMC and LiME account for 50 and 14 reversals, respectively, or 47.1% combined. The full artifact improves on ordinary outputs. The complete artifact outperforms ordinary outputs by 11.8 pp  (Table 6)  . Ordinary outputs also outperform raw code, demonstrating value in reusing execution work. Both handoffs come from separate upstream runs with comparable resource use. The comparison evaluates protocol-guided construction and its resulting handoff. Code and environment removal cause the largest losses, showing the need for repaired implementations and compatible dependencies. Removing the guide or launchers also reduces success when code and environment remain available: an executable codebase can still leave settings, measurement rules, and entry points implicit. Retained components can partly compensate for removal (Appendix D.4). These losses favor pairing executable support with explicit guidance on measuring results. 4.6. Gains persist across Auditors despite imperfect detection Sensitivity to the Auditor. Codex and Claude inspect the same numerically matching outcomes in the first evaluation  (Table 7)  . Appendix presents the human-review protocol and additional audit cases. 4.7. Repeated reuse can offset construction API cost Constructing the 36 artifacts costs $5,026 in API usage ($139.61 per paper). At the mean downstream costs in Table 3, break-even requires 8, 13, and 9 reuse rounds for Sonnet 4.6, Sonnet 5, and Opus 5, respectively. Each round repeats all 36 papers; the scenario charges the full construction cost to one model, holds prices and savings fixed, and excludes GPU, auditing, and 13 ReproBridge: Building Reproducibility into ML Research Artifacts maintenance costs. The corresponding API savings are $653, $409, and $615 per complete reuse round, respectively. Higher success accompanies these savings, so reuse improves reproduction while progressively recovering the construction investment. Appendix details the accounting rates and break-even calculation. 5. Related work Scientific trust and computational reproducibility. Scientific trust depends on collective scrutiny and accessible evidence (Munafò et al., 2017; Nosek et al., 2015; Oreskes, 2019); AIassisted research retains these requirements (Messeri and Crockett, 2024). Following ACM terminology, reproducibility means independent execution of authors artifacts, rather than independent reimplementation or bitwise-identical replay (Association for Computing Machinery, 2020; Peng, 2011). Reproducibility Enhancement Principles and the NeurIPS reproducibility program promote explicit dependencies, code release, and reporting checklists (Pineau et al., 2021; Stodden et al., 2016). Research reproduction benchmarks. PaperBench assesses reconstruction through expert rubrics covering code, execution, and results (Starace et al., 2025); SciReplicate-Bench also studies implementation reconstruction (Xiang et al., 2025). REPRO-Bench and ReplicationBench extend assessment to social science and astrophysics (Hu et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025). COREBench tests execution of released Code Ocean capsules and questions about their outputs (Siegel et al., 2024). ReproBridge-Bench evaluates released artifacts through binary task success, combining intervals based on variability across five human-verified executions with an independent integrity audit. Tasks include GPU training and evaluation. Table 4 compares handoffs under CORE-Benchs scoring rule. Automated reproduction and reusable experience. PaperCoder constructs repositories through planning and code generation (Seo et al., 2026). AutoReproduce recovers implicit details from cited papers and evaluates execution fidelity (Zhao et al., 2026b). VERITAS executes research procedures and produces patched code, fix records, and claim assessments (Liu et al., 2026a); our external comparison tests reuse of its handoff. Reflexion retains verbal feedback, while Voyager accumulates executable skills (Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023). The Compiler for Agent-Native Research Artifacts (ARA) (Liu et al., 2026b) packages papers and repositories with expert rubrics in its PaperBench study; model judge scores reproduction against those rubrics. We construct runnable four-component handoffs without evaluation rubrics or human reference scores, and assess their value through four component removals and an ordinary-outputs control. 6. Discussion and limitations The four component contracts make reproduction experience reusable, and ReproBridge-Bench provides verified reference scores for evaluation. We study their roles together; the delivery protocol guides what ReproBridge recovers and preserves during construction. In the formulation of Section 2.1, the aim is to reduce avoidable deviations 𝐷 while documenting uncertainty about the intended experiment. 6.1. Use before submission and by later reproducers The primary intended use is for authors to apply ReproBridge as reproducibility check before submitting paper and releasing its artifacts. Executing the papers specified setup can expose missing details, execution barriers, and papercode inconsistencies, giving authors concrete issues 14 ReproBridge: Building Reproducibility into ML Research Artifacts to inspect and correct before submission. Third-party reproducers can likewise preserve their work in the same format to lower the cost of later attempts. human reader can use the setup route and launchers to execute experiments, then inspect the guide and change record to assess the settings and repairs. Our experiments measure reuse by coding agents. 6.2. Papercode misalignment When the paper and released code conflict, ReproBridge strictly follows the papers setup and flags the discrepancy with source locations and affected tasks. For example, the Manifold-Aware Perturbations guide identifies learning rate of 104 in the paper versus 103 in the released code. Such records help authors check consistency between their manuscript and implementation during the pre-submission review described above. separate agent-assisted static analysis records 238 in-scope contradiction findings touching 669 distinct selected tasks. contradiction requires an explicit paper statement and conflicting implemented behavior; absent implementations and choices on which the paper is silent are recorded separately. These findings are possible sources of execution deviation 𝐷, but their effects on measured performance require controlled comparisons. They are neither human-validated error rates nor explanations of the measured gains. The analysis is separate from primary success scoring, and its records were not supplied to evaluated Reproducers. Appendix D.6 documents the scope, categories, and evidence. 6.3. Limitations The evaluation conditions on retained papers, fixed reference regions, and the tested agents; it is not conference-wide reproduction rate. Five reference observations are protocol choice, not guarantee of adequate uncertainty estimation. Numerical compatibility does not certify scientific validity or complete fidelity to the stated experiment, and refined artifacts can preserve incorrect assumptions. Automated audits also miss some violations, as quantified against human verification. The complete artifact intervention includes upstream investigation, repair, review, and packaging. Ordinary outputs and refined artifacts are produced in separate runs with comparable upstream resource use. This comparison evaluates the construction workflow and resulting handoff together; it does not isolate the effect of reorganizing identical outputs. Component ablations measure losses conditional on the remaining materials. Case annotations and variability strata describe patterns rather than isolate causal effects. API savings concern downstream Reproducer sessions. Construction, independent verification, GPU execution, maintenance, and human review have separate costs; reuse estimates assume fixed prices and savings. Human time savings and comprehension require separate study. 7. Conclusion ReproBridge standardizes recovered reproduction procedures and decisions into four reusable components: refined codebase, environment setup, experiment launchers, and reproduction guide. ReproBridge-Bench provides verified reference scores to assess their value. Reproduction success depends jointly on artifact quality and reproducer ability. All four evaluated models achieve mean reproduction success above 90% with refined artifacts, including those with lower raw-code success. The cross-model success-rate spread and downstream API spending both decrease. Removing code or environment setup causes the largest ablation losses; removing guides or launchers also reduces success with the other components retained. 15 ReproBridge: Building Reproducibility into ML Research Artifacts Future work should evaluate reuse by human researchers and measure the full costs of constructing, verifying, and maintaining artifacts across repeated attempts.

sections.title: AI use statement
sections.content: Coding agents constructed the refined artifacts, performed downstream reproductions, and produced automated integrity audits as part of the experiments (Sections 3 and 4.1). They also assisted human reference reproducers with setup, debugging, and script preparation under human verification (Appendix A.3). Agent-assisted reviews annotated recovered outcomes and papercode discrepancies; these annotations are descriptive and do not establish causal effects or human-validated error rates (Appendices D.2 and D.6). We used generative AI to draft and edit text, write and check analysis scripts, and prepare figure designs that were redrawn as editable diagrams. The authors defined the research question, hypothesis, benchmark, workflow, and evaluation protocols; reviewed all AI-assisted work; and checked the reported numbers and statistical plots against the recorded results and frozen analysis inputs. We did not use generative AI to generate synthetic data. The authors take responsibility for the final text, claims, and artifacts.

Construction-skill specifications ReproBridge implements artifact construction through role-specific skills, each with instructions, reference protocols, tools, and required outputs. Separate downstream Reproducer and Auditor workflows evaluate the artifacts; human reference collection and human audit validation belong to benchmark development and evaluation, respectively. Intake. Read the complete paper, including appendices, before planning. Preserve the selected task list and pinned raw commit. Map each task to its table entry, survey the implementation, check required artifacts, and record missing details. Do not silently substitute an unavailable repository revision or redefine task to fit the available code. Planner. For each task, specify the measurement, data, procedure, aggregation, and stated repetitions, with references to supporting paper passages or code locations. Group tasks that ReproBridge: Building Reproducibility into ML Research Artifacts share an execution. Record the adopted resolution of each ambiguity before the dependent run; prepare an executable plan and launcher. The Planner does not execute experiments. When paper and code conflict, strictly follow the papers stated setup, flag the conflicting code and affected tasks, and record the required implementation corrections before the dependent run. Builder. Resolve and record dependencies, provide reproducible acquisition of required data and checkpoints, and test the resulting environment. The environment described by the deliverable should be the one used for construction measurements, not an untested reconstruction assembled afterward. Environment work must not silently change the experimental plan. Construction Reproducer. Execute planned experiments in the prepared environment. Link values to actual output files and record commands, resources, and failures. Distinguish diagnostic runs from scored repetitions; justify changes and repetition extensions. Do not silently edit frozen plan or select favorable repetitions in place of the specified reporting statistic. Every task needs supported measurement or an explicit, evidenced reason why none was produced. Distiller. Write the guide and change record from stored task specifications, execution evidence, repairs, and choices. Explain the reporting statistic, observed variability, resource requirements, pitfalls, and uncovered scope. Preserve uncertainty where the record does not resolve it. Historical measurements belong in separate result records, not in instructions substituting for new measurements. Packager. Assemble the code, environment, launchers, and documentation actually used. Check portable paths and verify the handoff from clean shell, including an inexpensive real repetition. Compare the output structure and extraction route with the record. Do not invent replacement values or treat successful smoke test as completion of scientific experiment. Reviewer. Check the plan before scored execution, inspect evidence and recorded changes during reproduction, and test the final handoff as an unfamiliar user. Inspect the underlying files and outputs directly instead of accepting another roles summary. Produce localized findings with the responsible role; do not repair and approve the same work in one context. Alignment extension.
